notes.meaning: The person who lives close to God is pictured as living in His private, hidden room and resting in His shade. God is called the Most High, which means He is above everyone, and the Almighty, which means He has all power. Such a person is not just a visitor. They have a home under God's care. The 'secret place' may point to the inner room of the temple, where God's presence was. Now all who trust in Christ may come near to God.

The writer makes this truth his own: 'my refuge, my fortress, my God.' It is a small comfort to say 'God is a refuge.' It is a great comfort to say 'He is my refuge.' Saying it out loud honors God and helps others to trust Him too. Other people may lean on idols or on themselves. God never lets down those who trust Him.

A fowler is a bird-catcher, and his snare is a hidden trap. It stands for dangers we do not see coming. The deadly plague is sickness that strikes without warning. God keeps His people from many such dangers, often before they even know about them. Many older writers also read this as God guarding the soul from Satan's traps and from the spreading sickness of sin.

God cares for His people the way a mother bird covers her chicks with her wings. Jesus used the same picture of a hen and her chicks. Feathers are soft but easy to break through, so the verse adds a stronger picture. God's faithfulness, His sure keeping of His promises, is like a shield and a strong wall. He is as gentle as a hen and as strong as a soldier in armor.

Danger comes at every hour, by night and by day. Some of it is hidden, like disease in the dark. Some of it is open, like an enemy's arrow or ruin at noon. The promise here is not only safety but freedom from fear. Faith keeps God's people from being too afraid, because nothing touches them except by their heavenly Father's will.

Even when crowds fall all around from sickness or war, God can keep His own safe. The danger may be right at their side and still not touch them. Older writers add a careful word. This is not a promise that no believer will ever get sick or die in a plague. It means that whatever comes is in God's hands and will turn out for their good.

God's people will watch and stay unharmed while God's justice falls on the wicked. It is like Israel on Passover night, kept safe while Egypt was struck. Believers see some of God's justice even in this life. They will see it fully on the last day, when all things are made known.

The promise is for those who have made the LORD their home. They live in Him, rest in Him and lean on Him. Trouble may still come, but it will not truly harm them. God sends it in love and uses it for their good, even when it hurts for now. His care reaches their whole household too. Spurgeon tells how these verses gave him calm and courage while visiting the dying during a deadly cholera outbreak in London.

God gives His angels orders to guard His people. They carry them the way a nurse carries a small child, keeping them from even small stumbles. The words 'in all your ways' mean the path of duty God has set for us. When Satan quoted these verses to tempt Jesus (Matthew 4:6), he left those words out. The angels belong to God, so the thanks and praise go to God, not to them.

Even the fiercest and sneakiest creatures will be crushed underfoot. The lion stands for strong, open enemies and the snake for hidden, tricky ones. Many read this of victory over the devil, who is called a roaring lion and the old serpent. Paul promised that God will soon crush Satan under believers' feet (Romans 16:20). Some see it fulfilled most fully in Christ.

Now God Himself speaks. He promises rescue to the one who loves Him and 'knows His name.' To know His name means to know who God is, as He has shown Himself to us. God does not say 'because he is perfect.' He points to things even weak believers have: love for Him and trust in Him. 'Set him on high' means God lifts him up out of danger's reach.

God's people keep calling on Him in prayer, and He promises to answer. His answer may not always be 'yes,' but He will give what is best. If He does not end a trouble right away, He stays with them in it, comforting and strengthening them. In the end He brings them out and gives them honor that comes from Him.

God gives His people a life long enough to finish the work He has for them, and they are content with it. A believer may die young and still be satisfied, while a wicked person is never satisfied, even with many years. 'Show him My salvation' looks past this life to the joy of heaven. Some older writers also see it as seeing the promised Savior, and some see the whole promise coming true in Christ's resurrection.
